text:
The Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), Arsenio Dominguez, issued the following statement, following an incident involving a cargo ship (TIHAMAH) which was hit by a projectile off the coast of Al Mokha, Yemen. Several seafarer fatalities have been confirmed.

“It is with sadness and regret to know that, once again, innocent seafarers have lost their lives in an indefensible attack on international shipping. I offer my deepest condolences to the families of those involved.

It is particularly troublesome that the most recent attack has taken place in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden area. I reiterate my call for shipowners and ship operators to thoroughly assess risks before transiting this and other regions and follow appropriate best management practices. Seafarers deserve to be protected and allowed to do their jobs in safety and security.

These continued attacks on shipping only serve to escalate tensions and threaten global supply chains on which everyone depends.

I also urge the immediate and unconditional release of all seafarers who continue to be held captive following piracy attacks in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region.

Ensuring seafarer safety is a fundamental obligation under international law and a shared responsibility of the global community.”

text:
The publication, Mapping the adoption process for new drop-in fuels, notes that these fuels can be blended with conventional marine fuels and used in existing engines, offering a potential way to reduce emissions across the existing fleet without major retrofits, infrastructure changes or early vessel retirement. However, it stresses that drop-in fuels alone will not meet shipping’s long-term decarbonization goals and will need to complement other alternative fuels.

According to the study, the adoption process is currently “unclear, fragmented, and time-consuming,” involving multiple stakeholders whose responsibilities can overlap or vary depending on the fuel, vessel, engine and operating conditions. Regulatory requirements can also differ across national and international frameworks.

The study emphasizes that the process is not necessarily linear. Activities can run in parallel, require repeated testing or involve feedback loops, while a fuel that completes the process can still face technical, operational or commercial difficulties before wider adoption.

The estimated duration of individual stages ranges from two months to several years. The report estimates that reaching a vessel trial can take a couple of years, while full standard development and commercialization could take up to a decade.

Trial costs typically start at around $100,000, while full commercialization of a new fuel could involve several million dollars across the stakeholders involved.

Multiple stakeholders involved

The adoption process requires coordination between a broad group of maritime and fuel-sector stakeholders. The report identifies five groups with approval responsibilities for onboard use or bunkering:

Shipowners and ship operators

Flag states

Insurers

Port authorities

Classification societies and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), which provide technical input

Fuel producers and traders, technical managers, superintendents, laboratories, engine test centers, crew members and cargo owners also contribute to the process.

Shipowners ultimately decide whether to conduct trials, while flag states and insurers require robust risk assessments and mitigation plans. Port authorities are responsible for approving bunkering operations, while classification societies and OEMs provide technical assessments concerning vessel systems, engines and fuel compatibility.

Supply and standards remain challenges

The report points to limited availability of mature drop-in fuels as another barrier. FAME and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) are already established for maritime applications, but their potential supply is significantly below shipping’s overall fuel demand.

Global production of FAME and HVO could reach approximately 68 million tonnes of oil equivalent by 2030, while shipping currently consumes around 210–230 million tonnes of oil equivalent annually. This gap is driving interest in additional options, including pyrolysis oil, hydrothermal liquefaction oil and cashew nutshell liquid.

However, several of these newer fuels are not currently covered by ISO 8217:2024, creating additional challenges around fuel specifications, testing and approval.

The study concludes that drop-in fuels can provide a practical near-term option for reducing shipping emissions, but wider adoption will require a more predictable and coordinated approval process.

Greater cooperation across the maritime and fuel value chains, clearer regulatory requirements, expanded testing capacity and greater sharing of operational experience could help accelerate their commercialization.

title: IMO Net-Zero Framework: A Critical Decision for Shipping's Climate Future
description:
Despite this, governments are still debating whether to strengthen or weaken the IMO’s climate measures for shipping.
The draft Net-Zero Framework, approved by the IMO in April 2025, remains the basis for negotiations.
The framework combines a greenhouse gas pricing mechanism with a Net-Zero Fund, with revenues helping countries transition to cleaner shipping.
Among the proposals, the weakest, submitted by Liberia, would shift the balance by emphasizing trading surplus units between ships and removing mandatory payments into a Net-Zero Fund.
Weakening the greenhouse gas pricing mechanism or the Net-Zero Fund would not make the transition cheaper but more uncertain, less equitable, and harder to deliver.
text:
Governments face a critical decision next month on whether to protect the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework or reopen a deal that took years to negotiate and risks becoming weaker with each compromise, according to Anais Rios, senior shipping policy officer at Seas at Risk, writing for Splash.

Read also: IMO Warns Ships to Avoid Strait of Hormuz After U.S. Strikes Iran

2026 has so far been marked by climate disasters, including record heatwaves and severe wildfires in Europe, devastating floods in Southern and Western Africa, and increasingly destructive climate extremes worldwide. Despite this, governments are still debating whether to strengthen or weaken the IMO’s climate measures for shipping.

The draft Net-Zero Framework, approved by the IMO in April 2025, remains the basis for negotiations. While not perfect, it is described as the most equitable and climate-ambitious framework agreed upon, yet momentum has stalled. Countries are now debating whether to adopt it as is, amend it, or replace it.

The framework combines a greenhouse gas pricing mechanism with a Net-Zero Fund, with revenues helping countries transition to cleaner shipping. It creates emission targets where ships outperforming their targets earn credits, while those falling short must buy credits or pay remedial charges. As targets tighten, the financial incentive to adopt cleaner fuels and technology grows.

The urgency is underscored by 2024 being the first year global temperatures exceeded 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Every fraction of a degree brings more extreme weather and higher costs for communities and economies.

Among the proposals, the weakest, submitted by Liberia, would shift the balance by emphasizing trading surplus units between ships and removing mandatory payments into a Net-Zero Fund. This would direct payments largely between companies, potentially weakening investment in zero- and near-zero emission fuels if buying credits becomes cheaper than upgrading ships.

Brazil’s proposal retains the framework’s architecture but delays the early decarbonisation reduction threshold in exchange for steeper reductions later. While this might make an agreement more politically acceptable by lowering short-term costs, it would delay critical early investment and postpone fund revenues, making the transition harder and more expensive.

Tuvalu’s most ambitious proposal would charge for all greenhouse gas emissions above zero, potentially raising over US$100 billion per year during the 2030s, compared with around US$12 billion under the current framework. However, it is politically contentious due to higher upfront costs and could face refusal from the US and petrostates.

All these proposals were submitted within the required deadline, making them eligible for adoption later this year. Japan’s proposal, submitted after the deadline, cannot be voted on this year. It would allow shipowners to direct part of their compliance payments to projects of their own choosing, reducing funding predictability and support for countries in need.

Australia, Canada, South Africa, and the United Kingdom agree to preserve the framework as agreed in April 2025, arguing that the climate crisis urgency calls for implementation rather than reopening negotiations.

The current framework, while imperfect, contains the foundations of a global system that rewards cleaner shipping, creates predictable investment signals, and supports countries that cannot do it alone. Weakening the greenhouse gas pricing mechanism or the Net-Zero Fund would not make the transition cheaper but more uncertain, less equitable, and harder to deliver.

As the climate crisis accelerates, the question is no longer whether shipping must decarbonise, but whether governments have the political courage to protect the framework they have spent years negotiating. The people and the planet cannot afford another year of delay.

The regulation had previously been expected to enter into force in Norway during 2026. However, the latest announcement indicates that the process will take longer than initially anticipated.

As is already known, Norwegian and Icelandic ports will continue to be treated as third-country ports for FuelEU purposes until the Regulation has been incorporated into the EEA Agreement and implemented in Norwegian law.

Until the Regulation enters into force under the EEA Agreement, only half of the energy used on voyages between a port of call in Norway or Iceland and a port of call in the EU will be counted for FuelEU compliance purposes. Energy consumed on voyages within Norway or between Norway and non-EU countries during this period will not be counted for FuelEU compliance purposes.

…said Marte Hustveit Hauge, Senior Legal Adviser at the Department of Legislation and International Relations at the Norwegian Maritime Authority.

As stated, Norwegian shipping companies operating cargo or passenger ships of more than 5,000 gross tonnage that call at EU ports, and are therefore already subject to the Regulation, have been assigned to various EU Member States for administrative oversight.

title: Time is running out for shipping's climate compromise - Splash247
description:
Governments must decide next month whether to protect the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework or reopen a deal that took years to negotiate and risks becoming weaker with every compromise.
Yet governments are still debating whether to strengthen, or weaken, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) climate measures for shipping.
In April 2025, the IMO approved the draft Net-Zero Framework (NZF) and it remains the basis for negotiations.
Instead of generating a dedicated fund to support a just and equitable transition, payments would largely flow between companies.
Weakening the greenhouse gas pricing mechanism or the Net-Zero Fund would not make the transition cheaper.
text:
Governments must decide next month whether to protect the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework or reopen a deal that took years to negotiate and risks becoming weaker with every compromise. Anais Rios, senior shipping policy officer at Seas at Risk, gives Splash readers an overview of the various submissions doing the rounds at IMO HQ in London.

2026 is, so far, the year of climate disasters. Europe has endured record-breaking heatwaves and one of its worst wildfires seasons in recent history. Southern and Western Africa are recovering from devastating floods, while communities around the world continue to face ever more destructive climate extremes. Yet governments are still debating whether to strengthen, or weaken, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) climate measures for shipping.

In April 2025, the IMO approved the draft Net-Zero Framework (NZF) and it remains the basis for negotiations. It’s not perfect. However, it is the most equitable and climate-ambitious framework agreed upon, yet momentum has stalled. Rather than moving towards an adoption, countries are now debating whether to adopt it as it stands, amend it, or replace it.

The NZF combines a greenhouse gas pricing mechanism with a Net-Zero Fund. Revenues help countries transition to cleaner shipping. The framework creates a system of emission targets. Ships that outperform their targets would earn credits, while those that fall short must either buy those credits or pay remedial charges. As targets become stricter over time, the financial incentive to adopt cleaner fuels and technology grows.

The urgency to clean up shipping has never been greater. 2024 was the first year in which global temperatures exceeded 1.5oC above pre-industrialised levels. This is a stark warning of the direction we are heading. Every fraction of a degree brings more extreme weather, greater pressure on food and ocean systems, and higher costs for communities and economies alike. So why are governments still debating whether to weaken a framework that has already been approved at the IMO?

The weakest alternative proposal, submitted by Liberia, would significantly change the balance. Rather than relying on a combination of emission trading and fixed remedial payments, it would place greater emphasis on trading surplus units between ships and remove mandatory payments into a Net-Zero Fund. Instead of generating a dedicated fund to support a just and equitable transition, payments would largely flow between companies. If buying emission credits becomes cheaper than upgrading ships, then investment in zero to near-zero emission fuels would also become weaker.

Another proposal from Brazil retains the overall architecture of the NZF but delays the early decarbonisation reduction threshold in exchange for steeper reductions later. While this may make an agreement more politically acceptable by lowering short-term costs, delaying would not just affect climate reduction ambition and early investment in zero- and near zero-emissions that are critical in this decade, risking the transition before it has properly begun. It would also postpone revenues to the fund, making the transition harder and more expensive for all than under the current approved NZF.

Tuvalu’s has put forward the most ambitious proposal, requiring all greenhouse gas emissions above zero to incur a charge. Estimates suggest it would raise more than US$100 billion per year during the 2030s, compared with around US$12 billion per year under the current NZF, meaning that shipping would meet IMO’s decarbonisation targets whilst generating the funds needed for a just and equitable transition. However, the proposal is politically contentious as it would impose higher costs from the outset and could be refused by the US and petrostates.

All of the above proposals were submitted to the IMO within the required deadline, making them eligible for adoption later this year.

Japan has also tabled its own proposal that would allow shipowners to direct part of their compliance payments towards projects of their own choosing, rather than contributing to a dedicated IMO fund for a just and equitable transition. This would make funding less predictable, reduce support to countries in need; and risk slowing the transition, making it more expensive over time. However, because Japan’s proposal was submitted after the deadline, it cannot be voted for adoption this year.

Meanwhile, Australia, Canada, South Africa and the United Kingdom agree to preserve the Net-Zero Framework as agreed on in April 2025, arguing that the urgency of the climate crisis calls for implementation rather than reopening negotiations.

The current framework is not perfect. It is unlikely to deliver every emission reduction needed to meet IMO’s climate goals, and it will need to – and can – be strengthened over time. But it already contains the foundations of a global system that rewards cleaner shipping, creates predictable investment signals and supports countries that cannot do it alone.

Countries can and should debate the pace of implementation and level of ambition. Now, the framework is ready to be adopted. Weakening the greenhouse gas pricing mechanism or the Net-Zero Fund would not make the transition cheaper. It would make it more uncertain, less equitable, and harder to deliver.

As the climate crisis accelerates around us, the question is no longer whether shipping must decarbonise. It is whether governments have the political courage to protect the framework they have spent so many years negotiating. The people and the planet cannot afford another year of delay.

text:
Port of Long Beach approves "CAAP Plus" measures including enhanced green ship incentives

$40 million committed to a regional zero-emissions truck charging network

Approval comes days after congressional resolutions targeting California's At-Berth and harbor craft waivers

Port of Los Angeles board votes on the same measures August 13

New board president Steven Neal flags nuclear standards work with MARAD as port expands electricity, hydrogen, and methanol use

The Port of Long Beach has approved a package of new clean air measures, including enhanced incentives to attract the cleanest oceangoing vessels, just days after lawmakers in Washington moved to strip California of its authority to mandate shipping emissions rules.

The port's Board of Harbor Commissioners voted unanimously on August 10 in favour of the "CAAP Plus" measures, developed with the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), which approved them on August 7, with the Port of Los Angeles board scheduled to vote on August 13.

The three strategies include enhancements to the ports' existing green ship incentive programmes, which reward the cleanest vessels calling at the San Pedro Bay complex, alongside $40 million in new funding for a regionwide zero-emissions truck charging network and a further truck deployment incentive scheme.

The timing makes for an interesting contrast with pressures coming from the federal level.

As Ship & Bunker previously reported, last week Republican lawmakers filed resolutions in Congress to overturn the federal waivers behind California's At-Berth shore power rule and its renewable diesel mandate for harbor craft,

However, the Clean Air Action Plan is voluntary, and therefore untouched by the waiver fight, meaning incentive programmes of this kind could end up carrying more of the load if the state's mandatory rules fall.

The ports say the plan has delivered reductions of 90% in diesel particulate matter, 68% in nitrogen oxides, and 98% in sulphur oxides from port-related sources since 2005.

"As we prepare to handle 20 million TEUs by 2050, we are building the Port of the Future — a 100% zero-emissions port," Dr Noel Hacegaba, CEO of the Port of Long Beach, said in a statement.

"This new set of clean-air strategies strengthens our commitment, accelerates the zero-emissions transition and ensures cleaner air across the South Coast Air Basin."

The vote came on the same day Steven Neal began his one-year term as president of the port's harbor commission, pledging to advance its plan to double cargo to 20 million TEUs annually by 2050 while becoming a fully zero-emissions seaport.

Neal pointed to the port's growing use of electricity, hydrogen, and methanol for clean energy, and noted its recent partnership with the US Department of Transportation's Maritime Administration (MARAD) to develop operational, safety, and security standards for deploying nuclear energy in port operations.

"As global trade continues to expand and the demand for reliable, clean energy grows, we have an opportunity to lead — not simply by adapting to change, but by helping shape it," Neal said.

The new measures form an addendum to the Cooperative Agreement between the two ports and SCAQMD adopted last December, with the first phase of the ports' zero-emissions infrastructure plans expected in spring 2027.

text:
TUI Cruises has supplied its newest cruise ship, Mein Schiff Relax, with 1,875m³ of bio-LNG at the Port of Barcelona, marking the vessel’s first use of the renewable fuel.

The operation was completed in late July through ship-to-ship bunkering, with fuel transferred from the Haugesund Knutsen barge operated by Knutsen Scale Gas and chartered by Shell.

The bio-LNG was supplied from Enagás’ regasification plant at the Barcelona port, where it was produced and certified under the ISCC EU sustainability standard. The locally sourced fuel represents a short supply chain, with production and bunkering taking place within the same port area.

For TUI, the operation is a step towards its target of becoming climate neutral by 2050. Bio-LNG can deliver greenhouse gas emissions reductions of between 70% and 100% compared with fossil fuels, depending on the organic waste used to produce it, while its compatibility with existing LNG infrastructure allows Mein Schiff Relax to use the fuel without modifications to its dual-fuel engines.

Commenting on the achievement, Wybcke Meier, CEO of TUI Cruises, said: “With the bio-LNG bunkering of Mein Schiff Relax, we are demonstrating that we are already reducing CO2 emissions thanks to modern propulsion systems.

‘We are consistently pursuing decarbonisation and see alternative fuels as a key lever for achieving our climate reduction targets.”

What is bio-LNG?

Bio-LNG is liquefied biomethane produced from organic waste, including materials that would otherwise require disposal or treatment.

Organic matter is processed to produce biogas, which can then be upgraded to biomethane and cooled to cryogenic temperatures to create a liquid fuel.

Its significance for shipping comes partly from its compatibility with existing LNG technology. Because bio-LNG has the same basic chemical composition as fossil LNG, vessels equipped with suitable dual-fuel engines can use it without major changes to their propulsion systems.

The fuel could therefore provide a way for sectors such as maritime transport to reduce emissions while alternative technologies and fuels continue to develop.

Its overall climate benefit, however, depends on factors including the feedstock used, how it is produced and the emissions associated with its supply chain.

Mein Schiff Relax uses existing dual-fuel technology

Mein Schiff Relax is the first vessel in TUI Cruises’ new InTUItion class and forms part of one of the world’s younger cruise fleets. Like the company’s other newbuilds, it has dual-fuel engines designed to accommodate lower-emission fuels such as bio-LNG.

The approach is intended to give the fleet greater flexibility as cleaner marine fuels become available. Mein Schiff 7, which entered service in 2025, is also equipped for the potential future use of green methanol.

The Barcelona bunkering therefore demonstrates how alternative fuels can be incorporated into existing vessel operations without requiring a fundamental change to the ship’s propulsion system.

Bio-LNG forms part of wider climate strategy

TUI Cruises’ use of bio-LNG is one element of a broader strategy aimed at reaching climate neutrality by 2050. The company’s approach combines alternative fuels with other measures intended to reduce energy demand and emissions.

These include increasing the use of green shore power, improving energy efficiency through route optimisation and digital performance tools, and using hull coatings and cleaning systems to reduce resistance. Travel planning is also being adjusted to help limit overall energy consumption.

The company is also targeting waste reduction. Its measures include eliminating around five million plastic cocktail sticks and 10 million drinking straws annually.

title: EU approval paves way for Beijing Convention to enter into force on 15 December
description:
The Convention will enter into force for the EU on 15 December 2026.
Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 7 December 2022, the Convention entered into force internationally on 17 February 2026.
What EU approval means The EU’s approval is significant, but its effect is limited by the division of competences between the EU and its Member States.
As a result, EU approval does not by itself make the Convention fully applicable across all EU Member States.
The EU’s approval could nevertheless provide further momentum for the Convention.
text:
The European Union has approved the United Nations Convention on the International Effects of Judicial Sales of Ships, known as the Beijing Convention, marking a further step towards a common international framework for the recognition of judicial sales of vessels.

The EU deposited its instrument of approval on 18 June 2026 and reiterated the declaration it made under Article 18(2) when it signed the Convention. The Convention will enter into force for the EU on 15 December 2026.

Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 7 December 2022, the Convention entered into force internationally on 17 February 2026. It was prepared by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), building on a draft convention on the recognition of foreign judicial sales of ships developed by the Comité Maritime International (CMI) and approved by the CMI Assembly in 2014.

The United Nations Convention on the International Effects of Judicial Sales of Ships, also known as the “Beijing Convention on the Judicial Sale of Ships”, establishes a harmonized regime for giving international effect to judicial sales, while preserving domestic law governing the procedure of judicial sales and the circumstances in which judicial sales confer clean title.

By ensuring legal certainty as to the title that the purchaser acquires in the ship as it navigates internationally, the Convention is designed to maximize the price that the ship is able to attract in the market and the proceeds available for distribution among creditors, and to promote international trade.

What EU approval means

The EU’s approval is significant, but its effect is limited by the division of competences between the EU and its Member States. As highlighted by the International Bar Association, under its declaration of competence, the EU becomes a party to the Convention only in areas falling within EU competence.

The Member States retain responsibility for the remaining provisions. As a result, EU approval does not by itself make the Convention fully applicable across all EU Member States.

As explained, the distinction is particularly relevant given the current state of ratification. The UN Treaty Collection records 34 signatories and five parties. Within the EU, Spain has ratified the Convention, while Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Italy, Luxembourg and Malta have signed but not yet ratified it.

The EU’s approval could nevertheless provide further momentum for the Convention. It confirms support for the international regime at EU level and establishes the EU’s position on the relationship between the Convention and existing EU rules, including those governing jurisdiction and the service of documents.

For the Convention to take full effect at national level, however, individual Member States that have not yet become parties will still need to ratify or accede to it. As highlighted, the EU’s approval is limited to the areas covered by its declaration of competence, specifically Articles 4 and 9, and only to the extent that those provisions may affect common EU rules or alter their scope.

text:
German cruise operator TUI Cruises has expanded its use of bio-liquefied natural gas (bioLNG), with two vessels now operating entirely or substantially on the renewable fuel across European cruises.

The company’s dual-fuel Mein Schiff Relax vessel is running on bioLNG for its Northern European itineraries during the 2026 summer season.

BioLNG is also being used to fuel Mein Schiff Flow, which has been bunkering the fuel in Barcelona since May.

According to TUI Cruises, bioLNG use had resulted in around 26,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) equivalent greenhouse gas savings compared with conventional marine fuels by July 2026.

The company projects that the reduction will reach approximately 50,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent by the end of the year, according to Chief Executive Wybcke Meier.

The use of bioLNG is supported by the fact that it can be used as a drop-in fuel in existing LNG-fuelled engines and transported, stored and bunkered using existing LNG infrastructure, according to a study by Nanyang Technological University’s Maritime Energy and Sustainable Development Centre of Excellence.

The 2022 study found that bioLNG could deliver up to 80% greenhouse gas emissions reductions compared with marine diesel, although it stressed that methane leakage during production and methane slip from ships’ engines must be minimised.

Last year, Norwegian cruise operator Havila Voyages powered one of its ships with bioLNG in what was described as the first cruise using entirely liquefied biogas.

Early calculations predicted that the vessel would reduce its actual CO2 emissions by almost 92% through the use of biogas and the ship’s battery pack.

BioLNG use also eliminates a large amount of sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides, while working with existing LNG ships and port infrastructure without requiring engine retrofits.

However, the climate benefits of gas-based marine fuels remain subject to scrutiny, particularly around methane emissions.

Sustainability-leaning NGO Transport & Environment has highlighted methane leakage across the LNG supply chain and methane slip from ship engines as key factors that can undermine the climate benefits of gas-fuelled vessels.

“Sustainability is in our hearts. We made good progress last year,” said TUI Group CEO Sebastian Ebel during an earnings call. “Of course, it gets always more challenging in the next year, but we are well on track to deliver our 2030 targets.”

text:
Shipowners need to rethink several common assumptions around FuelEU Maritime and biofuels, according to maritime software and data services firm NAPA.

The company has outlined seven common myths facing the industry, with FuelEU Maritime and biofuels among the areas where it believes operators need to rethink their approach, according to an article published on its website on Sunday.

Ossi Mettälä, product manager, shipping solutions at NAPA, said there is no longer plenty of time to develop a FuelEU strategy, with the regulation already in its implementation phase and compliance requirements set to tighten over time.

Operators that achieve over-compliance can also create commercial value through banking and pooling mechanisms.

FuelEU Maritime Is a Commercial and Operational Strategy Question

Banking allows surplus compliance to be carried forward, while pooling allows vessels to combine compliance balances to offset individual deficits or surpluses.

He also challenged the belief that biofuels are always too expensive.

While their spot prices are generally higher than conventional fossil fuels, Mettälä said operators need to consider the wider cost of compliance.

For vessels operating within or into the EU, EU ETS costs and FuelEU Maritime penalties can change the economics of biofuels and make them commercially viable in some cases.

“Essentially, in a changing regulatory environment, looking only at headline fuel cost can lead to the wrong conclusion,” Mettälä said.

The remaining five myths cover weather routing, wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) and older vessels.

Mettälä said weather routing is no longer too complex or time-consuming for crews.

Modern systems combine weather forecasts, vessel performance models and operational restrictions to optimise voyages within minutes.

The company also rejected the idea that weather routing is unnecessary on fixed or short-sea routes.

Changing weather and sea conditions can affect safety, arrival times and fuel consumption even on repeat voyages.

Wind Propulsion Moves Beyond Experimental Stage

Mettälä said WAPS have moved beyond the experimental stage, with fuel savings already being recorded depending on the technology, vessel and operating conditions. Weather routing can help maximise those savings by identifying favourable wind conditions.

He addd said owners should assess the expected payback of WAPS for each vessel before installation and independently verify savings before deploying the technology across a wider fleet.

NAPA also challenged the view that older ships do not need investment in performance monitoring. Older tonnage remains subject to requirements including the IMO Carbon Intensity Indicator and FuelEU Maritime.

Performance monitoring can identify where efficiency is being lost and help owners improve existing vessels without relying solely on costly retrofits, alternative fuels or early replacement.

Mettälä said the industry should focus on practical technology, reliable data and vessel-specific analysis when making decarbonisation decisions rather than relying on assumptions about fuel prices or the capabilities of existing technologies.

text:
The International Maritime Organization's (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, shipping's proposed binding scheme to price and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, has spent the past ten months in a state of repeated delay, shifting coalitions and open disagreement over its core architecture. With the next negotiating session due in September and a further vote expected around November, this is a fuller account of how the dispute has unfolded and where it currently stands.

What the NZF Actually Is

The Net-Zero Framework combines a global fuel standard, requiring ships to progressively reduce greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) on a well-to-wake basis, with a carbon pricing and reward mechanism, designed to be added as a new Chapter 5 to MARPOL Annex VI. It would apply to all ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, covering roughly 85% of international shipping's CO2 emissions. Fleets that outperform the GFI standard can sell Surplus Units to fleets that fall short; underperforming fleets that don't buy enough Surplus Units instead pay a Remedial Unit penalty, with proceeds flowing into an IMO Net-Zero Fund intended to support zero and near-zero fuel uptake and a "just and equitable" transition for developing states.

April 2025: Approval, But Not Adoption

Member states approved the NZF as draft MARPOL amendments at MEPC 83 in April 2025, by a vote of 63 in favor, 16 against, and 24 abstentions. Approval at this stage set the text as the basis for formal adoption, but did not itself bring the framework into force; that step was scheduled for an extraordinary session later in the year.

October 2025: The Adjournment, and Who Moved

That extraordinary session, MEPC/ES.2, met from 14 to 17 October 2025 to consider formal adoption. Instead, a motion to adjourn the decision by one year, tabled by Singapore and brought to a vote by Saudi Arabia, passed 57 votes to 49, with 21 abstentions and 8 delegations absent, pushing the formal adoption vote to October 2026. The voting breakdown revealed significant shifts from the April approval: China, which had not blocked approval in April, voted for the delay in October; Japan and South Korea abstained, both reversing what had been supportive positions in April; and EU member states Greece and Cyprus also abstained, a break from the EU's usual bloc unity on climate measures that raised questions about how firmly united European support for the framework actually was. Multiple reports described unusually intense lobbying and political pressure surrounding the vote, atypical for the IMO's normally consensus-driven process, with the US, Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states reported among those pushing for delay.

May 2026: MEPC 84 Confirms the Foundation, But Not the Details

At MEPC 84, held in the following spring, member states agreed that the NZF's original architecture would remain the foundation for continued negotiations, alongside consideration of alternative proposals, rather than being discarded outright. Discussions remained divided on key design elements, particularly the structure of the Net-Zero Fund, and no decisions on core NZF design features were reached at this meeting; delegates instead agreed to hold additional intersessional meetings to continue the technical and political work.

The Alternative Proposal Now on the Table

Argentina, Liberia and Panama, three states that together flag more than 30% of the world fleet by gross tonnage, have circulated a joint alternative proposal intended to replace the approved NZF text. It would remove mandatory carbon pricing and the Remedial Unit penalty structure, tie GHG fuel intensity targets to the actual cost, availability and market share of low-emission fuels rather than fixed reduction trajectories, rely solely on Surplus Unit trading as the compliance mechanism, and eliminate the IMO Net-Zero Fund. The proposal's backers argue the currently approved GFI threshold is too restrictive, estimating it could generate GHG penalties of up to USD 300 billion by 2035, disproportionately borne by small and medium-sized operators.

Where the Opposition Is Concentrated

The US, Saudi Arabia and Russia were among the states most associated with pushing for the October 2025 delay. Separately, industry and technical voices, including a submission from the Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) on 6 August 2026, have pushed for the ongoing dispute to be resolved on the basis of comparative technical evidence rather than purely political negotiating positions, ahead of the next Intersessional Working Group session (ISWG-GHG 22) running 1-4 September 2026.

Why This Matters Beyond Shipping Itself

Whether a UN body can hold together a binding, global carbon-pricing mechanism at all, in the face of sustained political pressure from major economies, is the broader question this dispute tests. The outcome will shape how shipowners, fuel suppliers and investors plan around alternative marine fuel adoption over the next several years, and whether a genuinely global standard emerges or the industry instead operates under a patchwork of regional schemes such as the EU ETS and UK ETS, each with different rules and timelines.

text:
Bills introduced in Congress to attack California’s shipping waivers

In Washington, Congress introduced resolutions that attack two of California’s shipping waivers, the Ocean-Going Vessels At Berth and Commercial Harbor Craft waivers. For 50 years, the precedent set under both Democratic and Republican administrations is that the Clean Air Act waivers are not rules. text:
Summary

On 6 July 2026 the Government published a revised National Policy Statement for Ports (NPSFP), replacing the one designated in 2012. It keeps the same basic architecture, a presumption in favour of consent and a market-led approach, but builds on it in ways that matter for anyone bringing forward port capacity. Offshore wind gets real policy weight for the first time, hydrogen and ammonia are named as commodities ports should plan for, and the need case now runs to 2050.

Why the new npsfp matters

National policy statements such as the NPSFP are key to the certainty of the fast-track development consent regime set up by the Planning Act 2008. Where a proposed port scheme meets the thresholds in that Act, for example a container terminal capacity increase above 500,000 twenty-foot equivalent units or a bulk traffic increase above five million tonnes a year, it needs a development consent order. The Secretary of State must decide that application in accordance with the NPSFP unless doing so would breach an international or statutory duty, be unlawful, or mean the adverse impacts of the scheme outweigh its benefits. The NPSFP also carries weight beyond DCOs. It is a relevant consideration for the Marine Management Organisation when it decides harbour orders and marine licences, and it may be material for local planning authorities dealing with port-related applications under the Town and Country Planning Act 1990.

What is the same

The 2026 NPSFP is not a complete rewrite. It explicitly says that it updates and enhances the 2012 NPSFP to reflect changed circumstances and policy, rather than replacing its underlying approach. The core architecture survives: judgments on when and where development occurs are still to be made on commercial factors in a free-market environment, there is still a compelling need for new capacity and there is still a presumption in favour of granting consent for compliant development.

What has changed

What has moved is the scale of what that need now covers and the sectors it is built to serve.

The 2026 NPSFP concludes a compelling need for substantial additional port capacity over the next 30 years, referring to updated Department for Transport demand forecasts running out to 2050 but setting out scope for these to be replaced by new forecasts. Containers, ro-ro and dry bulk are all expected to grow. Liquid bulk is the exception, forecast to fall as the energy mix moves away from oil and toward lower-carbon commodities.

The presumption in favour of consent is now stated in more explicit terms. Port development that falls within the established need and complies with the statement's policies benefits from that presumption. Alongside it sits a new instruction that decision-makers should give substantial weight to the positive impacts of economic development.

The bigger shift is in what the need case now covers:

The 2012 NPSFP's energy section covered oil, liquefied natural gas and biomass. The 2026 NPSFP adds hydrogen and ammonia as commodities ports should be planning to handle, and treats ensuring security of energy supplies through ports as an essential consideration rather than simply an important one.

Offshore wind has moved from a passing mention to a central theme, with a statement that ports should not be disadvantaged by avoidable delay in the planning system. Floating offshore wind in particular gets its own recognition for the first time too, with an acknowledgement that it needs deeper water, heavier lift capacity and more laydown space than conventional turbines, meaning new, bespoke port facilities.

Cruise and passenger traffic also gets a stronger platform, with a dedicated tourism and leisure section and specific economic contribution figures included for the first time.

Biodiversity net gain is built into the NPSFP for the first time too, applicable to the onshore and intertidal parts of a scheme. A future Biodiversity Gain Statement is expected to set out how this will work for nationally significant projects once the relevant provisions of the Environment Act 2021 are commenced.

Key takeaways

The policy foundation for promoting NSIP port capacity has widened beyond freight and bulk. Port scheme DCO applications built around supporting energy transition infrastructure such as offshore wind, including floating offshore wind, or hydrogen, ammonia and other next generation energy commodities now have an express foothold in the NPSFP.

Cruise and passenger operations are in a stronger position too. International sea passenger numbers to and from UK ports were already back above 23 million a year by 2023, and the cruise sector alone is credited with contributing £9.4 billion to the UK economy and supporting 82,000 jobs, figures the NPSFP now sets out expressly to back a sector it says has kept growing since the pandemic.

The explicit presumption in favour of consent, backed by the new substantial weight to be given to economic benefits, will be key to the case for all applicable schemes.

text:
The global shipping industry could approve rules this year to impose a kind of levy on polluting vessels. If implemented, the measure would change the fuel mix used in shipping worldwide and accelerate decarbonization, but it would also put pressure on freight rates. Companies in the sector have been preparing for the transition for years, but final approval of the rules remains uncertain because of opposition from the U.S. government.

“Companies had been moving aggressively to transition to alternative fuels, and now they have slowed down,” said Leandro Barreto, a partner at Solve Shipping. He expects the rules to be approved in the near term, but said the U.S. stance has undermined market confidence that this will happen this year. “The agenda will not be abandoned, but it may be delayed,” he said.

War and cheaper technology drive green fuels in transport

Logistics plan envisions R$1.2tn in investment by 2050

Brazil airlines face sustainable fuel rollout amid supply, cost concerns

In 2023, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) approved significant greenhouse gas reduction targets: emissions must be cut by at least 20% by 2030. By 2050, the goal is to reach net-zero emissions.

The industry is now discussing the introduction of a financial charge on greenhouse gases emitted by ships, while vessels with a lower environmental impact would be rewarded. Once formally adopted, the rule is expected to take effect after a 16-month transition period.

At the end of last year, there was an expectation that the rules would be formally adopted. However, the U.S. blocked the discussions, which were subsequently postponed until the end of this year.

According to the IMO’s latest study, published in 2020, maritime transport emitted 1.08 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2018. The sector accounted for 2.89% of global carbon dioxide emissions caused by human activity.

The cost of decarbonization, however, is a concern. The market expects the adoption of the rules to increase freight rates, at least initially.

If the new rules are adopted, there could be an additional charge of up to $380 per tonne of carbon equivalent—equivalent to roughly $200 more per tonne of fuel consumed, estimates Luis Resano, executive director of the Brazilian Coastal Shipping Association (Abac).

Alternative fuels that would not be subject to the levy are not yet competitive. “There is currently no fuel available at scale to replace oil. At the same time, prices fall as production increases,” Barreto said.

According to Resano, the alternative being developed by Petrobras in Brazil is bunker fuel blended with 24% biodiesel. This option is 20% to 30% more expensive than conventional fuel. “It is not economically viable. But if the IMO rules are approved, the higher cost will change the equation,” he said.

Barreto notes that Europe already charges a levy on polluting vessels, encouraging shipping companies to make changes, although the impact remains limited. “The European Union is driving the agenda. It is an important market, but it is not yet the largest.”

Shipping companies are already testing different alternatives. For Germany’s Hapag-Lloyd, in the short term, the most viable options are drop-in biofuels, which can be used in existing vessels without major modifications, such as biodiesel and biomethane.

“Methanol is an important next step, but the economics and infrastructure are still being developed,” said the company’s CEO, Luigi Ferrini. Ammonia is another option, but the technology is not yet mature and therefore would be a longer-term solution.

In addition to methanol, ethanol is also seen as an option. About a month ago, French shipping company CMA CGM carried out the first ethanol bunkering of a container ship in Brazil, at the Port of Santos.

Outside Brazil, Denmark’s Maersk is also testing the fuel. This year, the group announced the first voyage of a vessel powered entirely by ethanol.

Resano, however, says it will be important to ensure that the IMO accepts sugarcane ethanol, which faces opposition in Europe. The argument there is that fuel made from food crops creates risks to food security and deforestation. Brazilian companies, however, see the criticism as an attempt to block a solution that is not produced by the European market. “We have to make sure ethanol will be considered a valid fuel,” said Abac’s executive director.

In short-sea shipping, he considers biodiesel the main short-term alternative. “Because it is a dual-fuel and does not require changes to the vessel, it is the best solution. We have been talking to producers, and there is capacity to serve the market,” he said.

Petrobras says it has the capacity to supply B24, a blend containing 24% biofuel. The product is already being distributed at the Port of Rio Grande in Rio Grande do Sul state. So far in 2026, 3 million liters of bunker fuel with renewable content have been delivered at the port. “Our operational supply capacity is significantly higher than these volumes, allowing us to meet growing demand,” the company said. Petrobras also said it will be ready to supply B24 at the Port of Santos later this year.

Beyond this solution, the state-owned oil company is studying other projects involving LNG, bio-LNG and e-methanol, it said.

Electrification is not considered as attractive an option for ships because batteries take up a great deal of space and would reduce cargo capacity, Resano said.

Ferrini of Hapag-Lloyd said that, in addition to alternative fuels, the company has been investing in efficiency measures that also reduce emissions—including hull and propulsion improvements that lower operating costs, as well as reducing vessel speeds, which saves fuel.

Along with adapting their fleets, shipping companies will also face significant changes in where they can refuel. “Alternative fuels will initially be available only at selected ports, concentrating bunkering at certain multifuel hubs, such as Rotterdam and Singapore, and this will force companies to plan services around these locations,” Ferrini said. This new dynamic could even change shipping routes and the port calls currently made by carriers.

In the cruise industry, one of the main bets is on ships with engines capable of running on diesel, LNG, and their sustainable alternatives. “Today, 58% of new ships are multifuel,” said Marco Ferraz, president of Brazil’s Cruise Lines Association (CLIA).

According to Ferraz, multifuel engines are gaining ground mainly because of the lack of standardization in fuel availability. Brazil has no LNG infrastructure at its ports. Although it is not a biofuel, LNG is viewed as a transition technology because it produces about 20% fewer emissions.

text:
Nicosia, Cyprus. Shipping companies in Cyprus and Greece could face significantly different carbon costs depending on which of four proposals is adopted by the International Maritime Organisation, with options ranging from no direct greenhouse gas charge to a Tier 1 compliance price of $300 per tonne of CO2 equivalent.

The outcome could affect Cyprus’ shipmanagement cluster and the Greek-owned fleet, including operating costs, charter agreements, investment in cleaner fuels and the commercial viability of older vessels.

Existing European requirements

Companies operating through European ports are already paying under the EU Emissions Trading System and complying with FuelEU Maritime.

The prospect of an IMO mechanism has raised concerns that companies could face overlapping charges for the same emissions.

IMO framework

The framework, approved in principle in April 2025 but not yet legally binding, combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism.

It would apply to ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnes, which account for more than 85 per cent of the international shipping emissions covered by the IMO.

Tuvalu proposal

Tuvalu has proposed tripling the price of Tier 1 remedial units from $100 to $300 per tonne of CO2e while retaining the Tier 2 price at $380.

The Pacific island state also proposes a 100 per cent direct-compliance threshold from 2029 to 2035 and the removal of surplus units. Ships exceeding greenhouse gas fuel-intensity limits would therefore make payments into the IMO Net-Zero Fund rather than buy credits from better-performing vessels.

Tuvalu’s proposal would retain the base fuel-intensity targets but remove the 2028 step, beginning the trajectory with a 6 per cent reduction in 2029. The plan would place a price on all emissions from that year and create the largest revenue pool for cleaner fuels and support for vulnerable developing countries.

However, it would also result in the highest initial rise in transport costs, particularly for vessels unable to secure suitable low- or zero-emission fuels at commercially workable prices.

The first data on FuelEU Maritime compliance is now emerging, following the first year of reporting against greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity targets for shipping companies trading in the EU.

To better understand what the early results show, we spoke with Joe Bettles, Climate Policy Manager and author of the Countdown newsletter at the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping (Center). The Center recently published its analysis of the first reporting year in the article “What did we learn from the first year of FuelEU?”

Under the regulation, shipowners have several options for compliance, including:

A. The pooling mechanism, which allows vessels with a compliance surplus to trade it with other vessels.

B. The borrowing mechanism, which allows companies to defer a compliance deficit to the following year for a 10% surcharge.

C. Meet the target by using low GHG intensity fuels.

D. Pay the FuelEU penalty (penalty).

Pooling becomes the preferred option

The first year of reporting indicates that pooling has quickly become the preferred choice. According to data from the European Commission, 92% of vessels used the pooling mechanism, while only 2% used borrowing. The remaining vessels either paid the penalty or met the target by using LNG or other low-GHG energy sources.

Commenting on the findings, Joe Bettles says: “Our insights from the first year of reporting indicate that shipping companies were able to comply with the targets, with most using the pooling mechanism. This shows that FuelEU is working as intended. As we approach the IMO’s upcoming discussion on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), FuelEU demonstrates that it is possible for the global fleet to comply with a GHG intensity regulation using existing fuels and providing incentives for the uptake of cleaner energy sources.”

A developing market for compliance surplus

The Center’s article also reviews the different pooling platforms available to shipping companies seeking to meet their obligations under the regulation. The price of compliance surplus, averaging around EUR 208/tCO₂eq, remained relatively stable, suggesting that the market matured early, with buyers generally able to find sellers.

On the development of the pooling market, Joe notes: “The prices for trading compliance surpluses remained well below the EUR 640/tCO₂eq penalty for VLSFO, making the pooling mechanism significantly more attractive than paying the penalty.”

Fuel choices remain central to compliance

The role of fuel choice is also important. Looking at fuels supplied to the FuelEU market, the Center estimates that 3.22 million tCO₂eq of reductions, relative to an all-VLSFO fleet, will be required to meet the 2% reduction target between 2025 and 2029. Based on analysis of previous years’ fuel consumption, the Center indicates that LNG may have contributed around one-third of the required reduction. Biofuel blends account for the remainder, with biodiesel and bio-LNG dominating the low-GHG fuel mix.

Joe highlights how the pooling mechanism can help extend the impact of lower-GHG fuels across the fleet: “Although LNG is not a drop-in replacement for VLSFO, the pooling mechanism under FuelEU allows an LNG-fuelled vessel to share its over-compliance with other vessels that cannot physically use LNG. Depending on the engine type in the ship, LNG can remain compliant with the 14.5% reduction target through 2039 and can further extend its compliance through banked surplus or by using liquified biomethane.”

Three early lessons from FuelEU Maritime

Drawing on the first year of reporting, Joe Bettles and the Center identify three lessons that may also be relevant for the IMO in the future.

First, the results indicate that a fuel standard for shipping can work. FuelEU’s first year has created incentives for the use of alternative fuels and a market for those who prefer to pay for emissions compliance.

Second, regulations should include mechanisms that support a broader mix of energy sources. Lower-maturity alternatives, such as wind-assisted propulsion, e-fuels and onshore power, still represented a limited share of the mix.

Third, policy stability and clear reduction pathways can help reduce uncertainty for shipping companies and support the business case for investment in cleaner alternatives.

Supporting knowledge sharing across the maritime value chain

Skuld is a Mission Ambassador to the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping, supporting its work as a platform for collaboration, knowledge sharing and practical insight across the maritime value chain.

“The Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping is a highly valuable forum for us at Skuld. It provides access to a broad network of industry stakeholders and helps us stay close to the challenges shipowners face in meeting regulatory requirements and reducing emissions. Just as importantly, it serves as a platform for dialogue and knowledge sharing across the maritime value chain“ – Matias Bøe Olsen, Decarbonisation and transition risk lead, Skuld.

You can read the full article on FuelEU’s first-year experiences here: https://www.zerocarbonshipping.com/news/countdown-what-did-we-learn-from-the-first-year-of-fueleu

title: Cyprus shipping firms await crucial IMO decision on global carbon pricing
description:

text:
Shipping companies in Cyprus and Greece could face a radically different carbon bill depending on which of four rival proposals prevails at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), with the options ranging from no direct greenhouse gas charge to a Tier 1 compliance price of $300 per tonne of CO2 equivalent.

The outcome directly concerns Cyprus’ shipmanagement cluster and the Greek-owned fleet, affecting operating costs, charter agreements, investment in cleaner fuels and decisions over whether older vessels remain commercially viable.

It also comes as companies operating through European ports are already paying under the EU Emissions Trading System and complying with FuelEU Maritime, creating fears that a future IMO mechanism could expose them to overlapping charges for the same emissions.

At the centre of the negotiations is a question with a very expensive answer, how much should a ship pay for its pollution, and who will ultimately pick up the bill?

The proposals now heading into the next round of talks could take the IMO framework in sharply different directions.

Approved in principle in April 2025 but not yet legally binding, the framework combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism. It would apply to ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnes, which account for more than 85 per cent of the international shipping emissions covered by the IMO.

At the strictest end of the debate is Tuvalu, which wants the price of Tier 1 remedial units tripled from $100 to $300 per tonne of CO2e, while retaining the Tier 2 price at $380.

The Pacific island state is also proposing a 100 per cent direct-compliance threshold from 2029 to 2035 and the removal of surplus units. As a result, ships exceeding the required greenhouse gas fuel-intensity limits would have to make payments into the IMO Net-Zero Fund rather than purchase credits from better-performing vessels.

Tuvalu’s proposal would keep the base fuel-intensity targets but remove the 2028 step, beginning the trajectory with a 6 per cent reduction in 2029. In practice, the plan would place a price on all emissions from that year and produce the largest pool of revenue for cleaner fuels and support for vulnerable developing countries.

However, it would also result in the highest initial increase in transport costs, particularly for vessels unable to obtain suitable low or zero-emission fuels at a commercially workable price.

Liberia, whose flag is used by a large number of Greek-owned ships, is pushing in almost the opposite direction.

Its proposal, building on an earlier submission with Argentina and Panama, would remove direct greenhouse gas pricing and the purchase of remedial units. Instead, compliance would depend on tradable surplus units that shipping companies could transfer, bank or borrow.

Fuel-intensity targets would also be determined according to the cost, availability and market share of lower-emission fuels, with the trajectory recalculated every five years rather than tied directly to the checkpoints in the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy.

The argument is that ships should not face heavy penalties when the cleaner fuels required for compliance are still unavailable in sufficient quantities or at competitive prices.

However, critics warn that relying heavily on traded credits could expose owners to volatile compliance costs and weaken the stable price signal needed to support investment in genuinely zero or near-zero-emission fuels. Removing payments into the Net-Zero Fund would also leave no clear mechanism for directing revenue towards developing countries affected by higher transport costs.

Between the two sides is Brazil, which is proposing a slower start followed by stricter requirements later.

Its plan would ease compliance during 2029 and 2030 by aligning the base and direct-compliance targets, before returning to the previously agreed trajectory from 2031. To compensate for the softer beginning, Brazil wants the longer-term base target tightened to 70 per cent in 2041, compared with 65 per cent in 2040 under the existing framework.

Meanwhile, Australia, Canada, South Africa and the United Kingdom are seeking to retain most of the original system, including its fuel-intensity targets and compliance prices, while adjusting the implementation dates to reflect the one-year delay in negotiations.

For Cyprus and Greek shipping companies, these differences go far beyond regulatory language.

A high global carbon price could change the financial picture of an individual vessel. Older ships with heavier fuel consumption may become considerably more expensive to operate and less attractive to charterers, while newer and more efficient tonnage could secure a stronger commercial advantage.

The final decision will therefore influence investments worth hundreds of millions of dollars that are being considered today. Shipowners must decide whether new vessels should be equipped with dual-fuel engines, which alternative fuels they should be capable of using and whether retrofits to existing ships will deliver sufficient returns.

The difficulty is that these decisions must be taken before companies know which fuel will become widely available, how much it will cost or how heavily conventional emissions will eventually be priced.

There is also the question of who pays. Under time-charter agreements, the charterer often controls the ship’s route, speed and fuel consumption, while responsibility for regulatory compliance may remain with the shipping company.

As carbon costs increase, charterparties will need to define more clearly who monitors emissions, purchases compliance units and bears the financial consequences when a vessel exceeds the required limits.

For companies trading through Europe, the calculation becomes even more complicated. The EU ETS already covers 100 per cent of emissions from voyages between EU ports and 50 per cent from voyages beginning or ending outside the bloc. FuelEU Maritime separately requires a gradual reduction in the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board.

If a global IMO mechanism is introduced without a clear reconciliation system, vessels could face different calculations, reporting requirements and liabilities for overlapping emissions.

Philippos Ioulianou, managing director of Cyprus-based EmissionLink, said, “Shipping should not pay twice for the same tonne of emissions. If the EU ETS operates alongside a future IMO carbon-pricing mechanism, there must be an automatic and transparent way to recognise payments and reconcile liabilities.”

EmissionLink has also called for at least 50 per cent of the EU ETS revenue generated by shipping to be reinvested in sustainable fuels, port infrastructure, vessel retrofits and credible energy-efficiency technologies.

The next stage of the debate will take place during intersessional meetings on September 1 – 4 and November 23 – 27, before MEPC 85 meets from November 30 to December 3.

text:
Japan says GFI targets should reflect the pace of fleet replacement.

New marine fuels are estimated to account for 5.8% of total fuel use in 2030.

Japan has proposed a less stringent path for greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) under the proposed IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF), saying the approach could address concerns about the impact of the targets on international shipping.

In a submission to the IMO ahead of further discussions in September, Japan said its revised draft amendments are intended to provide a basis for reaching a compromise among member states.

The proposal includes changes to the annual GFI reduction factors as well as the framework's compliance arrangements.

Under the proposed NZF, ships would have to meet two GFI levels: a base target and a more stringent direct compliance target. Japan retains the two-tier approach but proposes lower reduction factors for both.

For the base target, Japan proposes a 7% reduction in 2030, increasing to 21.9% in 2035. Its proposed direct compliance target rises from a 21% reduction in 2030 to 43% in 2035.

Using the document’s 2008 reference GFI of 93.3 gCO2e/MJ, those reductions translate to about 86.8 gCO2e/MJ in 2030 and 72.9 gCO2e/MJ in 2035. This compared to 85.8 gCO2e/MJ proposed in NZF for 2030 and 65.3 gCO2e/MJ in 2035.

Japan says some member states support GFI targets in line with the 2023 IMO GHG strategy, while others have concerns about their impact and feasibility.

It says “massive changes”, including early ship replacement and semi-mandatory major conversion, should be avoided.

The proposal takes account of the existing fleet. Japan says 95% of merchant ships were conventional-fuelled at the end of 2025 and argues that the replacement speed of existing ships should be considered when setting achievable GFI targets.

“It is necessary to find achievable GFI targets based on the replacement speed of existing fleets, using a performance-based approach,” Japan said.

Japan also proposes removing mandatory payments and the IMO Net-Zero Fund from the draft framework. Under its approach, ships would in principle comply through the use of low-emission fuels or surplus units (SUs).

Ships that cannot balance their compliance deficits with surplus units could instead make direct contributions to IMO-approved projects.

Japan says companies could also choose projects aimed at supporting particular new fuels or technologies.

The revised draft also removes the fixed GFI reduction factor for 2040. Japan says future targets should be reviewed periodically and take into account the global availability, affordability and scalability of new fuels and technologies.

Japan says its revised draft provides a possible basis for further discussions aimed at finding a final compromise among IMO member states.

name: Maritime Transport
title: What's wrong with FuelEU - Splash247
description:
Under Article 21 of the regulation, ships may pool compliance balances so the pool meets the greenhouse gas intensity limit on average.
Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1805, a FuelEU Document of Compliance confirms that a ship complied with the regulation for a reporting period.
The regulation puts the compliance duty on the company responsible for the ship, the fuel user.
FuelEU attaches the duty to the ship because the ship burns the energy.
What’s wrong with FuelEU is not that shipping was asked to cut emissions.
text:
Captain Alex Byelyavtsev identifies six problems with the controversial European regulation.

FuelEU Maritime was sold as a climate rule. Its job was to push ships toward renewable and low-carbon energy, and to help the EU’s Fit for 55 plan. The method is simple on paper. Each year the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used on board must fall. If it does not, there is a penalty. If the balance is accepted, the ship gets a Document of Compliance.

The first year showed something else. Under Article 21 of the regulation, ships may pool compliance balances so the pool meets the greenhouse gas intensity limit on average. That flexibility is written into the rule. A ship can look compliant through the pool, not only through its own fuel. Compliance can be collective.

That is the first problem. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1805, a FuelEU Document of Compliance confirms that a ship complied with the regulation for a reporting period. That can include pooling. It does not prove that the ship cut its voyage emissions or changed its fuel at scale. Compliance is an accounting result. Emission reduction is a physical result. Early FuelEU practice has mixed the two.

The second problem is the fuel. Clean marine energy is not ready at fleet scale. Drop-in biofuels are limited and contested. Methanol and ammonia help only ships that can burn them. Most of the world fleet still burns conventional bunkers. Yet the legal year can still end with a green balance. The Commission’s own impact assessment pathways said renewable and low-carbon fuels should provide 6% to 9% of the international maritime fuel mix by 2030, and 86% to 88% by 2050. Those are model paths, not today’s supply.

The third problem is who is obliged. The regulation puts the compliance duty on the company responsible for the ship, the fuel user. It does not put the same hard duty on producers to make that fuel at scale. It concentrates responsibility on the final user. An ICS and ECSA study warned that putting the main fuel-standard duty on ships, rather than fuel suppliers, creates enforcement and supply problems. The law can demand a cleaner fuel that does not yet exist in the volumes required.

The fourth problem is the target. Article 4 sets the cut at 2% from 2025, 6% from 2030, then much harder toward 80% by 2050. The dates are clear. For many ships, the physical path is not. The target is someday-achievable if the fuels appear, the ships are replaced and the money holds. Someday possible is not the same as achievable now.

The fifth problem is money. Real transition needs capital for new ships and scarce fuels. UNCTAD’s Review of Maritime Transport 2025 put the global containership fleet at about 30.3 million teu by April 2025, up about 10% year-on-year, after heavy ordering and elevated deliveries. Those ships add slots. More slots mean more competition. That squeezes the surplus available for the next round of transition.

The sixth problem is where responsibility sits. FuelEU attaches the duty to the ship because the ship burns the energy. Research on port congestion shows ships often sail fast, then wait at anchor for a berth, with average potential emissions savings of about 10% for containerships if waiting time becomes slower sailing. An IMO-backed Just in Time study found average fuel savings of about 14% per containership voyage when speed is matched to berth availability. FuelEU still parks the legal duty on the vessel.

Shipping is only about 3% to 4% of EU CO₂ on commission figures. It already faces ETS for shipping as well as FuelEU. The political noise is large for that share. The early paperwork success is large too. The real fuel change is still small.

What’s wrong with FuelEU is not that shipping was asked to cut emissions. It is the order of the rule. The EU set a mandatory transition for fuel users. It did not match that with a hard production duty at the same scale. It gave early flexibility that keeps ships legally compliant. It treated the compliance balance as the visible win. The fuels, the fleet and the funded path for real emission cuts are not ready at scale. A system can certify compliance without delivering transition. That is the gap the first year made clear.

name: Maritime Transport
title: INSIGHT: EU ETS Expansion Raises Critical Questions on Fairness and Effectiveness
description:
Image Credit: EmissionLink The European Commission's proposed expansion of the EU Emissions Trading System for maritime transport is an important development in regional climate policy.
In practice, however, offshore shipping does not fit neatly into a conventional port-to-port model.
The Commission's proposal to bring certain categories of vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the EU ETS from 2029 will also have significant implications.
However, these proposals do not resolve how the EU ETS will coexist with a future IMO carbon-pricing framework.
Ultimately, the credibility of the EU ETS will depend not on how much money it raises, but on whether it delivers fair treatment and meaningful emissions reductions for the industry which is expected to fund it.
text:
Philippos Ioulianou, Managing Director, EmissionLink. Image Credit: EmissionLink

The European Commission's proposed expansion of the EU Emissions Trading System for maritime transport is an important development in regional climate policy. Yet the real test is not whether the system becomes more expansive, but whether it becomes more coherent, proportionate and effective.

Two concerns stand out. The first is the risk of overlapping carbon-pricing regimes as the International Maritime Organization moves towards its own global mechanism. The second is the widening gap between the revenues shipping is expected to contribute and the amount reinvested in maritime decarbonisation.

These questions are especially relevant to shipping centres such as Greece and Cyprus. Across the Eastern Mediterranean, shipowners, managers and offshore operators face an increasingly demanding compliance environment. As their regulatory exposure grows, so does the commercial importance of understanding how carbon costs will be allocated, managed and recovered.

The planned inclusion of offshore activities from 2027 illustrates the challenge. Offshore worksites are set to be treated as ports of call, bringing more support-vessel activity within the ETS. In practice, however, offshore shipping does not fit neatly into a conventional port-to-port model.

Offshore vessels may remain on location for extended periods, serving projects where fuel use, operational control and emissions responsibility are divided among owners, charterers, contractors and developers. The ETS therefore becomes not merely a reporting issue, but a contractual and commercial one. Responsibility for monitoring emissions, acquiring allowances and bearing carbon-price exposure will increasingly need to be addressed in charterparties and project agreements.

The Commission's proposal to bring certain categories of vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the EU ETS from 2029 will also have significant implications. Many smaller commercial and offshore operators are likely to enter a system designed around larger organisations with dedicated compliance teams, established data processes and greater access to carbon-market expertise. Broader coverage may be justified, but implementation must remain proportionate.

There are welcome elements in the proposals. Greater alignment between MRV and FuelEU Maritime reporting should reduce duplication and the risk of inconsistent submissions. Changes to transhipment rules are also intended to limit circumvention and protect the system's integrity.

However, these proposals do not resolve how the EU ETS will coexist with a future IMO carbon-pricing framework. The Commission has acknowledged the possibility of double payment, but acknowledgement is insufficient. Applying regional and global charges to the same emissions without a clear reconciliation mechanism would create unnecessary costs and uncertainty.

Shipping should not pay twice for the same tonne of emissions. If both systems remain, there must be an automatic, transparent and workable method for recognising payments and reconciling liabilities. This should also apply to revenue allocation. Shipping is expected to contribute substantially to the ETS, yet only a limited share appears destined for maritime decarbonisation. This imbalance risks undermining confidence in the policy.

I would argue that at least 50% of ETS revenues generated by shipping should be reinvested in maritime decarbonisation at national level. Support should also be extended across sustainable fuels, port infrastructure, vessel retrofits and credible energy-efficiency technologies. Carbon pricing can reduce emissions only when matched by practical investment that enables the industry to move forward.

For shipping companies, the ETS is no longer simply a compliance requirement. It is a core commercial consideration affecting costs, contracts, investment decisions and competitiveness. Companies like EmissionLink, with a presence in Greece and Cyprus allows them to combine local market knowledge with specialist expertise, helping companies turn evolving emissions rules into practical compliance and commercial strategies.

Ultimately, the credibility of the EU ETS will depend not on how much money it raises, but on whether it delivers fair treatment and meaningful emissions reductions for the industry which is expected to fund it.
